titleStmt.title: Kleine Lieder für Kinder zur Beförderung der Tugend

work.title: Kleine Lieder für Kinder zur Beförderung der Tugend

history.p: In a letter to Karl Wilhelm Ramler dated late August 1765, Christian Felix Weiße mentions that he recently had been approached by his acquaintance Scheibe who wished to set music to some moral or educational poems for children. According to Scheibe’s introduction, he and his publishers Korte in Flensburg had for the past three years talked about remedying the lack of children’s songs. However, it should also be noted that Scheibe might indeed have been inspired by his friend, the composer Carl Heinrich Graun who published Zwölf Kindersonaten mit Liedern nach Graunschen Melodien in 1762. Weiße apparently liked the idea and sent two dozen poems to Scheibe. It was around the same time that Weiße had become a father, and having heard the tasteless songs sung by the wet nurse and child-carer he was inspired by the idea of writing a collection of new poems for children. Already in August 1765 Scheibe finished the introduction thus implying that also the songs were completed, and in January 1766 they were published with a dedication to Weiße’s wife, Christiane Elisabeth. Scheibe's introduction to the songs explains aspects of performance practice and audience. He also mentions that the collection has two purposes: 1) singing; and 2) playing the harpsichord. The following year, Weiße issued the poems in a revised version as Lieder für Kinder also adding new ones to the collection. Weiße’s poems were published again in 1768 (including an appendix) and again in 1770. The poems created an interest among intellectuals and educators, and the collection was reviewed in several German as well as Danish journals already in 1768.The first one, an anonymous review, appeared in Unterhaltungen already in 1766. The critique is rather severe, concluding that the beautiful poems deserved a better fate and that both children and adults should be spared the melodies. One of the later, known reviewers was the composer Johann Adam Hiller, and in 1769 he decided to use the same texts and published his Lieder für Kinder. Mit neuen Melodien. These were reviewed by Heinrich Wilhelm von Gerstenberg in Hamburgische Neue Zeitung (1769) who notes that 'a part of these songs was already composed in a larger form and that by a man who has undisputed merits regarding German music, among which the composition of his children’s songs cannot be included.' Hiller’s melodies are light, simple and natural. In 1775, Hiller issued a second edition, and now Scheibe is mentioned specifically: 'One has already seen the contemporary songs composed in a larger form by Mr. Kapellmeister in Copenhagen, and I was requested to present them on a smaller scale. To carry out this demand – and not to compare myself with another – I have composed new settings [of the poems].' A second collection appeared in 1768 (see SchW B5:Coll.003).

annot.p: 'Genug, die schönen Poesien hätten ein besseres Schicksal verdient. Wir ersuchen daher den Herrn Kapellmeister, im Namen des guten Geschmacks, künftig Kinder und Erwachsene mit dergleichen Melodien zu verschonen.'
A review which contains substantial quotations from Scheibe's introduction to the collection of children's songs.

annot.p: 'Ein Theil dieser Lieder war schon ehmals in größrer Gestalt componirt, und zwar von einem Manne, der um die deutsche Musik unbezweifelte Verdienste hat. Worunter aber die Composition seiner Kinderlieder nicht mit gerechnet werden kann.'

physDesc.physMedium: In 4o; oblong format, consisting of 8 bifolios nested in 2, 2, 2, 2; title page (fol. 1r; p. [1]), blank page (fol. 1v; p. [2]), music (pp. 3–29), single page of music (alternative version of SchW B5:101; no page number); in all 16 folios. Hand-ruled paper, 8 staves on pp. 1–23 and 9 staves on pp. 24–25 (8 mm; single rastrum used). Source contains some cancellations and revisions in ink (Scheibe); the first song, 'Der junge Baum' (SchW B5:101), appears in two versions (pp. 3, 30, corresponding to pp. 2, 3 in the printed edition).
In modern limp library binding; paper of a fairly dense quality.
